functions.name: Answering the phone

formal: Good morning, Hartley Dental. How may I help you?
Good afternoon, this is Maria speaking.
Hello, Sales Department. Can I help you?
neutral: Hello, this is Sam.
Hello? Who is calling, please?
Hi, Sam speaking.
informal: Hi there, go ahead.
Hey, it's me. What's up?
Yeah, hi. Who's that?

responses: Hello, this is Anna. Can I speak to Mr Brown?
Hi, is Tom there, please?
Hello. I would like some information, please.

example.en: Good morning, Hartley Dental. How may I help you?
Hello, I would like to speak to Dr Lee, please.
One moment, please. I will check.
Thank you.

avoid.right: Who is calling, please?
avoid.why: 'Who are you?' sounds rude on the phone. Ask who is calling.

functions.note: Say your name or the company name first. On the phone, say 'this is' for yourself, not 'I am'.

functions.name: Asking the price of something

formal: Excuse me, could you tell me the price of this?
How much is this item, please?
Could you tell me how much this costs?
neutral: How much is this, please?
How much are these apples?
What is the price of this bag?
informal: How much is this?
How much for one?
What does this cost?

responses: It is five pounds.
They are ten dollars each.
That one is twelve euros.

example.en: Excuse me, how much is this, please?
It is fifteen dollars.
Okay, I will take it.
Great. Cash or card?

avoid.right: How much is this?
avoid.why: Use 'much' for money and price, not 'many'.

functions.note: Use 'is this' for one thing and 'are these' for multiple items.

functions.name: Asking someone to repeat or speak more slowly

formal: Could you please repeat that?
Pardon me, could you speak more slowly?
Could you say that once more, please?
neutral: Can you repeat that, please?
Sorry, can you speak more slowly?
Could you say that again, please?
informal: Sorry?
Say that again?
One more time, please?

responses: Sure, no problem.
Of course. I said your train is at five.
Yes, sorry! I will speak slower.

example.en: Sorry, can you speak more slowly?
Of course. The bus arrives at ten o'clock.
Can you repeat that, please?
Sure, it arrives at ten o'clock.

avoid.right: Sorry, could you say that again?
avoid.why: 'What?' alone sounds abrupt and impolite to English speakers.

functions.note: Saying 'Sorry?' with rising intonation is a quick, natural way to ask someone to repeat what they just said.

functions.name: Asking where a place is

formal: Excuse me, could you tell me where the station is?
Pardon me, do you know where the restroom is?
Could you please direct me to the museum?
neutral: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?
Is there a bank near here?
Where can I find a pharmacy?
informal: Where is the bathroom?
Is the park this way?
Which way is the metro?

responses: Go straight and turn right.
It is next to the supermarket.
It is five minutes from here.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?
It is across the street, near the shop.
Is it far from here?
No, just two minutes away.

avoid.right: Where is the bus stop?
avoid.why: Singular countable places require an article like 'the' or 'a'.

functions.note: Start with 'Excuse me' before asking a stranger for directions.

functions.name: Greeting someone

formal: Good morning.
Good afternoon.
It is nice to see you.
neutral: Hello.
Hello, how are you?
Good to see you.
informal: Hi.
Hey!
Morning!

responses: Hello! Good to see you too.
Fine, thanks. And you?
Hi! I am good.

example.en: Good morning. How are you today?
Good morning! I am very well, thank you.
It is nice to see you.
Nice to see you too.

avoid.right: Good evening, how are you?
avoid.why: Use 'good night' only when leaving or going to sleep.

functions.note: Use 'Good morning' before 12:00 and 'Good afternoon' after 12:00. 'Hi' is the most common casual greeting.

functions.name: Introducing a friend to someone

formal: May I introduce my colleague, Anna?
I would like you to meet Anna.
This is Anna, our new team member.
neutral: This is my friend, Anna.
Anna, meet Sam. Sam, this is Anna.
Have you met my friend Anna?
informal: This is Anna.
Meet my buddy Anna.
Anna, this is Sam.

responses: Hello Anna, nice to meet you.
Hi Anna! Good to meet you.
Pleased to meet you, Anna.

example.en: This is my friend, Anna.
Hi Anna! Nice to meet you.
Anna, meet Sam. Sam, this is Anna.
Great to finally meet you.

avoid.right: This is my friend Anna.
avoid.why: Use 'this is' rather than 'here is' when introducing people.

functions.note: Use 'This is [Name]' when introducing someone standing next to you. It works in both social and work settings.

functions.name: Introducing yourself

formal: Hello, my name is Alex Reed.
Allow me to introduce myself, I am Alex.
Nice to meet you, I am Alex Reed.
neutral: Hello, I am Alex.
My name is Alex. Nice to meet you.
I am Alex. Pleased to meet you.
informal: Hi, I am Alex.
Hey, my name is Alex.
Hi there, call me Alex.

responses: Nice to meet you, Alex.
Pleased to meet you too.
Hi Alex, I am Sam.

example.en: Hello, I am Alex.
Nice to meet you, Alex. I am Sam.
Nice to meet you, too.
Welcome to our class.

avoid.wrong: I introduce myself, I am Alex.
avoid.right: Hello, my name is Alex.
avoid.why: We rarely say 'I introduce myself' in natural spoken English.

functions.note: Saying 'Nice to meet you' is standard after hearing someone's name for the first time.

functions.name: Ordering food and drink

formal: May I please have the chicken salad?
I would like a glass of water, please.
Could I have a coffee, please?
neutral: Can I have a tea, please?
I would like the soup, please.
A cheese sandwich for me, please.
informal: Just a coffee, please.
I'll have an apple juice.
Water for me.

responses: Of course. Anything else?
Sure, coming right up.
Small or large?

example.en: Hello, are you ready to order?
Can I have a tea, please?
With milk and sugar?
Just milk, please.

avoid.right: Can I have a coffee, please?
avoid.why: 'I want' sounds too direct and rude to servers.

functions.note: Always add 'please' at the end of an order to sound polite.

functions.name: Saying goodbye

formal: Goodbye. Have a nice day.
It was nice meeting you.
Have a pleasant evening.
neutral: Goodbye.
See you tomorrow.
Take care.
informal: Bye!
See you later!
Catch you later!

responses: Goodbye! You too.
See you tomorrow!
Bye, take care.

example.en: Goodbye. Have a nice day.
Thank you! You too.
See you tomorrow.
Yes, see you!

avoid.right: See you tomorrow.
avoid.why: You can only see someone again in the future.

functions.note: 'Bye' is friendly and safe in almost every everyday situation. 'Goodbye' sounds slightly more final or polite.

functions.name: Saying you do not understand

formal: Pardon me, could you repeat that?
I am sorry, I do not understand.
Could you speak more slowly, please?
neutral: I do not understand.
Sorry, what does that mean?
Can you say that again, please?
informal: Sorry?
What was that?
I do not get it.

responses: Sure, I said turn left.
No problem, let me explain.
Yes, I will say it again.

example.en: Take bus number twelve to the station.
I am sorry, I do not understand.
Take bus twelve. It goes to the trains.
Ah, okay. Thank you!

avoid.right: I do not understand.
avoid.why: Use 'do not' with the base verb 'understand', not 'am not'.

functions.note: Saying 'Sorry?' with rising intonation is very common and polite in everyday English.

functions.name: Saying sorry for a small mistake

formal: Please excuse me.
I beg your pardon.
Pardon me, please.
neutral: I am sorry.
Sorry about that.
I am so sorry.
informal: Sorry!
My bad!
Oops, sorry!

responses: No problem.
That is okay.
Do not worry about it.

example.en: Oops, sorry! I took your pen.
That is okay. I have another one.
Here it is. Thank you.
No problem at all.

avoid.wrong: I am sorry for drop your book.
avoid.right: I am sorry for dropping your book.
avoid.why: Use an -ing verb after the preposition 'for'.

functions.note: Use 'sorry' for everyday accidents. Keep your voice light so the other person knows it is not a serious problem.

functions.name: Saying thank you and replying

formal: Thank you very much for your help.
I am very grateful, thank you.
Thank you kindly.
neutral: Thank you very much.
Thank you for that.
Thanks a lot.
informal: Thanks!
Cheers!
Thanks a bunch!

responses: You are welcome.
No problem at all.
Anytime!

example.en: Here is your ticket and your change.
Thank you very much.
You are welcome. Have a nice trip.
Thank you, you too.

avoid.right: Thank you.
avoid.why: Say either 'thanks' or 'thank you', never combine them with an 's'.

functions.note: The standard reply to 'thank you' is 'you are welcome'.

functions.name: Accepting an apology

formal: Please do not worry about it. It was not a problem.
Thank you for apologising. I understand completely.
There is no need to apologise; these things happen.
neutral: That's okay, don't worry.
No problem. It happens.
It's fine, really.
informal: Forget it, no big deal.
Don't sweat it.
All good, honestly.

responses: Thanks for understanding.
That's kind of you.
I'll be more careful next time.

example.en: I'm so sorry I'm late. The bus was slow.
That's okay, don't worry.
Thanks. Have I missed much?
No, we have only just started.

avoid.right: That's okay.
avoid.why: 'You are welcome' answers 'thank you', not 'sorry'.

functions.note: If the problem was serious, you can add a reason to be kind, for example 'Everyone is late sometimes.'

functions.name: Accepting an invitation

formal: Thank you, I would be delighted to attend.
It would be a pleasure to join you.
Thank you, I accept with pleasure.
neutral: I would love to, thanks.
That sounds great, thank you.
Yes, I will definitely be there.
informal: Sounds good, count me in!
Yes, I would love that!
Awesome, see you there!

responses: Wonderful, see you then.
Great, I will send you the details.
Excellent, I look forward to it.

example.en: We are having lunch together. Would you like to come?
That sounds great, thank you.
Great, we are meeting at twelve.
Sounds good, see you there.

avoid.right: Yes, I would love to.
avoid.why: 'I like' talks about general hobbies; use 'I would love to' to accept an offer.

functions.note: After saying yes, show enthusiasm by adding a positive comment like 'That sounds great' or 'Thanks for inviting me'.

functions.name: Agreeing with someone

formal: I agree with you completely.
That is quite right, I think.
I could not agree more.
neutral: I agree with you.
Yes, that's true.
You're right about that.
informal: Yeah, totally!
Same here.
Exactly, that's what I think too.

responses: Great, so we think the same.
I'm glad you agree.
Good, let's do that.

example.en: I think this film is too long.
Yeah, totally! It was nearly three hours.
And the story was slow.
I agree. Let's watch something shorter next time.

avoid.right: I agree with you.
avoid.why: 'Agree' is a verb, so we do not use 'am' before it.

functions.note: Add a short reason after 'I agree' to sound more natural, for example 'I agree, it's too expensive.'

functions.name: Apologising

formal: Please accept my sincere apologies for the delay.
I apologise for any inconvenience caused.
I am extremely sorry for being late to the meeting.
neutral: I am really sorry about that.
Sorry for keeping you waiting.
I am sorry, that was my fault.
informal: Sorry about that!
My bad, I forgot.
Oops, sorry!

responses: That is quite all right, do not worry.
No problem at all.
It happens, do not worry about it.

example.en: I am really sorry about that.
No problem at all.
I dropped the glass by accident.
Do not worry, I will clean it up.

avoid.right: I apologise.
avoid.why: 'Apologise' is a verb, so do not use 'am' before it.

functions.note: Use 'I am sorry' for everyday mistakes, and save 'I apologise' for more serious situations.

functions.name: Asking for directions

formal: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the station?
Could you please direct me to the museum?
Pardon me, would you know where the post office is?
neutral: Excuse me, where is the nearest bank?
How do I get to the bus stop from here?
Is there a supermarket near here?
informal: Do you know where the park is?
Which way is the cinema?
Are we near the train station?

responses: Go straight on and turn left at the lights.
It is just around the corner on your right.
Sorry, I do not know this area.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the nearest bank?
Go straight on and turn left at the lights.
Is it far to walk?
No, it is only two minutes away.

avoid.right: Where is the hotel?
avoid.why: Singular countable nouns like hotel need an article such as the or a.

functions.note: Start with 'Excuse me' before asking a stranger for directions to sound polite.

functions.name: Asking for permission

formal: May I leave the room for a moment?
Would it be possible for me to use this phone?
Might I ask a question?
neutral: Could I borrow your pen, please?
Can I open the window?
Is it okay if I sit here?
informal: Can I have this?
Mind if I sit here?
Okay if I take one?

responses: Yes, of course.
Go right ahead.
I am sorry, but someone is sitting there.

example.en: Excuse me, is it okay if I sit here?
Yes, of course. Nobody is here.
Thank you very much.
You are welcome.

avoid.right: May I sit here?
avoid.why: Never use 'to' after modal verbs like 'may', 'can', or 'could'.

functions.note: Use 'May I' with teachers, managers, or strangers in formal situations.

functions.name: Booking an appointment by phone

formal: I would like to make an appointment, please.
Do you have anything available on Tuesday morning?
I would like to change my appointment to Friday.
neutral: Hello, I'd like to book a time for Monday.
Is the doctor free on Thursday?
Can I have a time after lunch?
informal: Hi, can I get in this week?
Got anything free tomorrow?
Is next Monday okay?

responses: Yes, we have a space at ten o'clock.
Sorry, we are full that day.
Can I have your name and number, please?

example.en: Hello, I'd like to book a time for Monday.
We have a space at ten o'clock. Is that fine?
Yes, that's perfect.
Can I have your name and number, please?

avoid.wrong: I want to make a reserve for Monday.
avoid.right: I'd like to book a time for Monday.
avoid.why: 'Reserve' is a verb here, and 'I want' sounds too direct on the phone.

functions.note: Say the day first, then the time. Spell your name slowly if the line is bad, and repeat the time to check.

functions.name: Checking in at a hotel

formal: Good afternoon, I have a reservation under the name of Smith.
Could we please check in? The booking is for two nights.
We have a room reserved under John Davis, please.
neutral: Hello, I would like to check in, please.
Hi, I have a booking under Anna Miller.
We are checking in, the name is Taylor.
informal: Hi there, checking in for Sam Brown.
Hi, we have got a room booked here.
Just checking in, name is Lee.

responses: Welcome. May I see your passport, please?
Here is your key card. Breakfast is on the first floor.
Your room is not quite ready yet.

example.en: Hello, I would like to check in, please.
Welcome. May I see your passport, please?
Sure, here it is.
Thank you. Here is your key card for room 204.

avoid.wrong: I want my key, I booked.
avoid.right: Hello, I have a booking, please.
avoid.why: Demanding a key sounds rude; state that you have a booking instead.

functions.note: Give your surname clearly when checking in so staff can find your booking quickly.

functions.name: Declining an invitation politely

formal: Thank you, but I am unable to attend.
I appreciate the invitation, but I have another commitment.
I am sorry, but I cannot make it that day.
neutral: I am sorry, but I cannot come.
I would love to, but I am busy then.
Thanks for asking, but I cannot make it.
informal: Sorry, I cannot make it.
I cannot, I have plans.
Wish I could, but I cannot.

responses: No problem, maybe next time.
That is okay, thanks for telling me.
Do not worry about it.

example.en: Are you coming to my dinner party on Friday?
I would love to, but I am busy then.
That is okay, thanks for telling me.
Have a wonderful time anyway!

avoid.wrong: I cannot come because I don't want.
avoid.right: I cannot come, but thank you.
avoid.why: Stating that you do not want to go sounds very rude.

functions.note: Always thank the person before or after saying no so you remain polite.

functions.name: Disagreeing in a simple way

formal: I am afraid I do not agree.
I see it differently, I am afraid.
I am not sure that is correct.
neutral: I don't agree with that.
I don't think so.
I see it differently.
informal: Hmm, I'm not so sure.
Nah, I don't think so.
No way, really?

responses: Oh, why do you think that?
Okay, that's fair.
Really? Tell me more.

example.en: I think winter is the best season.
Hmm, I'm not so sure. It's too cold for me.
But I love the snow.
Okay, that's fair. I like summer more.

avoid.wrong: I am not agree with you.
avoid.right: I don't agree with you.
avoid.why: 'Agree' is a verb, so make it negative with 'don't'.

functions.note: Say 'I'm afraid' or 'I'm not sure' first to sound softer. A plain 'No, you're wrong' can sound rude.

functions.name: Giving directions

formal: Go straight on, and the station is on your left.
Turn right at the traffic lights, and you will see it.
It is about five minutes from here on foot.
neutral: Go straight and turn left at the bank.
Take the second street on the right.
It's next to the post office.
informal: Just keep going, you can't miss it.
Hang a left at the corner.
It's right over there, across the road.

responses: Thank you, that is very clear.
Sorry, could you say that again?
Is it far from here?

example.en: Excuse me, where is the library?
Go straight and turn left at the bank.
Is it far from here?
No, it's about five minutes on foot.

avoid.wrong: Go straight until you will see the bank.
avoid.right: Go straight until you see the bank.
avoid.why: After 'until' we use the present simple, not 'will'.

functions.note: Give one step at a time and use landmarks such as a bank or a corner. 'On foot' means walking.

functions.name: Inviting someone out

formal: Would you care to join us this evening?
I would like to invite you to dinner.
Would you be interested in attending?
neutral: Would you like to come with us?
Do you want to see a film tonight?
Are you interested in joining us?
informal: Do you fancy a coffee?
Come to the cinema with me!
Want to grab some lunch?

responses: I would love to, thank you.
Sure, that sounds fun.
I am sorry, but I am busy.

example.en: Would you like to come with us to the park?
I would love to, thank you.
Great, we are leaving in ten minutes.
Perfect, I will get my coat.

avoid.wrong: Do you want go to the cinema?
avoid.right: Do you want to go to the cinema?
avoid.why: Remember to include 'to' before the main verb after 'want'.

functions.note: Use 'Would you like to...' as a polite and safe standard invite for both friends and colleagues.

functions.name: Making a plan to meet

formal: Would tomorrow suit you?
Could we schedule a time to meet?
What time would be convenient for you?
neutral: Are you free this afternoon?
Can we meet at two o'clock?
What time works best for you?
informal: Do you want to hang out later?
Let us meet after lunch.
Are you free later?

responses: Yes, that time is fine.
Two o'clock works for me.
I cannot make it then, sorry.

example.en: Are you free this afternoon?
Yes, I am free after three o'clock.
Can we meet at four at the cafe?
Yes, that time is fine. See you then.

avoid.right: Can we meet tomorrow at five?
avoid.why: Use 'can' or 'shall' to make a question for future plans.

functions.note: Always confirm the exact time and place at the end of the conversation so both people agree.

functions.name: Making a polite request

formal: Could you please assist me with this?
Would you mind helping me, please?
May I trouble you for some assistance?
neutral: Could you help me, please?
Can you please pass that to me?
Could you tell me the time, please?
informal: Can you give me a hand?
Pass me that, please.
Help me with this, will you?

responses: Of course, here you go.
Sure, I can do that.
I am sorry, but I cannot right now.

example.en: Excuse me, could you help me, please?
Sure, what do you need?
I cannot find the tea bags.
They are right here on shelf two.

avoid.right: Could you give me that book, please?
avoid.why: Using an imperative alone sounds like an order instead of a request.

functions.note: Use 'could' instead of 'can' when you want to sound more polite.

functions.name: Making a suggestion

formal: May I suggest that we meet on Friday?
Perhaps we could ask the manager for advice.
Would you like to visit the museum first?
neutral: Why don't we take the train?
Shall we have lunch now?
How about meeting at six?
informal: Let's grab a coffee!
We could just stay in tonight.
What about a pizza?

responses: Good idea!
I'm not sure. What else could we do?
Sounds great to me.

example.en: Why don't we take the train?
Good idea. It's cheaper than a taxi.
And we can look at the view.
Sounds great. Let's leave at nine.

avoid.wrong: Why we don't go by bus?
avoid.right: Why don't we go by bus?
avoid.why: In a question, the helper verb 'don't' comes before 'we'.

functions.note: After 'Why don't we', 'Shall we' and 'Let's', use the base verb: Why don't we go? Let's go.

functions.name: Offering help

formal: May I assist you with that?
Would you like any assistance today?
Please let me know if I can help you.
neutral: Can I help you with anything?
Do you need any help?
Would you like a hand with that?
informal: Need a hand?
Want me to do that?
Let me help you.

responses: Yes, please. That is very kind.
No, thank you. I am fine.
Thanks, I can manage.

example.en: Those boxes look heavy. Would you like a hand with that?
Yes, please. That is very kind.
Where should I carry them?
Just put them on the table, thanks.

avoid.wrong: I must help you with your bag.
avoid.right: Can I help you with your bag?
avoid.why: Do not force help on people; ask questions to give them a choice.

functions.note: Saying 'Need a hand?' is common and friendly among coworkers and friends.

functions.name: Reporting a simple problem

formal: I am afraid there seems to be a problem with the air conditioning.
Excuse me, I believe there is an error on our bill.
Pardon me, the television in my room does not appear to be working.
neutral: Excuse me, the shower is not working.
There is a problem with my order, this is cold.
This shirt is damaged, look at this mark.
informal: The Wi-Fi is down again.
This soup is cold.
The light will not turn on.

responses: I am so sorry, I will fix that right away.
Let me speak to the manager about that.
I will bring you a fresh one immediately.

example.en: Excuse me, the shower is not working.
I am so sorry, I will fix that right away.
Thank you, there is no hot water.
I will send someone to your room now.

avoid.right: The machine is not working.
avoid.why: Use the negative verb 'is not working' to describe a broken item.

functions.note: Start with 'I am afraid' or 'Excuse me' to report problems politely without sounding angry.

functions.name: Saying what you like and dislike

formal: I am very fond of classical music.
I do not care for crowded places.
I particularly enjoy walking in the countryside.
neutral: I like tea, but I don't like coffee.
I really enjoy cooking.
I'm not keen on spicy food.
informal: I love pizza!
I can't stand loud music.
Football's not really my thing.

responses: Me too!
Oh, really? I don't like it.
What do you like to drink?

example.en: Do you like spicy food?
I'm not keen on spicy food. I prefer mild dishes.
Really? I love it.
I can't stand it when my mouth burns!

avoid.right: I like pizza.
avoid.why: Verbs of feeling, like 'like', are not used in the continuous form.

functions.note: After 'like', 'love', 'enjoy' and 'can't stand' we can use a noun or a verb with -ing: I enjoy cooking.

functions.name: Asking for another size or returning an item

formal: Could I please exchange this item for a larger size?
I would like to return this shirt, please.
Could you tell me if you have this in medium?
neutral: Do you have this in a size ten?
Can I try this on in a smaller size?
I want to return this, please.
informal: Got this in a bigger size?
Can I swap this for a small?
Can I bring this back if it does not fit?

responses: Let me check the stockroom for you.
Yes, do you have your receipt?
I am sorry, we have sold out of that size.

example.en: Do you have this in a size ten?
Let me check the stockroom for you.
Thank you, I will wait here.
Here you go, we had one left.

avoid.right: I want to exchange this shirt.
avoid.why: Use 'exchange' with 'to', or say 'swap' in casual speech.

functions.note: Shops usually ask for a receipt when you want to return or swap an item.

functions.name: Small talk about the weekend

formal: Did you have a pleasant weekend?
I hope you had a relaxing weekend.
Are you doing anything special this weekend?
neutral: How was your weekend?
Did you do anything nice?
Any plans for the weekend?
informal: Good weekend?
What did you get up to?
Doing anything fun on Saturday?

responses: It was lovely, thanks. We went to the beach.
Not much, just relaxed at home.
I'm visiting my parents. And you?

example.en: How was your weekend?
Lovely, thanks. We went to the beach.
Oh, nice! Was the water cold?
Very! What did you do?

avoid.right: How was your weekend?
avoid.why: The weekend is finished, so we use the past tense 'was'.

functions.note: Always ask the question back. Answering with just one word can end the chat, so add one small detail.

functions.name: Asking for advice

formal: I would appreciate your advice on a matter.
What would you recommend in this situation?
Could I ask for your guidance on how to proceed?
neutral: What should I do?
Can I ask your advice about something?
What would you do in my place?
informal: Got a minute? I need some advice.
Help me out here, what would you do?
Any tips?

responses: Of course. What's the problem?
Well, what are your options?
I think I'd take the offer.

example.en: Can I ask your advice about something?
Of course. What's the problem?
I have two job offers. What would you do in my place?
I'd take the one with better training.

avoid.right: Can you give me some advice?
avoid.why: 'Advice' is a noun, and 'advise' is the verb. Say 'give advice' or 'advise me'.

functions.note: 'Advice' has no plural. Say 'some advice' or 'a piece of advice', never 'advices'.

functions.name: Asking for clarification

formal: Could you clarify what you mean by that?
I am not sure I follow. Would you mind explaining it again?
Could you be more specific about the deadline?
neutral: Sorry, what do you mean exactly?
Can you explain that a bit more?
Do you mean the first or the second option?
informal: Wait, what do you mean?
Sorry, you lost me there.
Hang on, can you say that another way?

responses: Sure, let me put it another way.
What I mean is that we need it by Friday.
Of course. Which part is unclear?

example.en: Please send the report as soon as you can.
Sorry, what do you mean exactly? Is today too early?
What I mean is that I need it by Friday.
Got it. I'll send it on Thursday.

avoid.wrong: What do you mean by this word is?
avoid.right: What do you mean by this word?
avoid.why: After 'What do you mean by', put the thing, not a new verb 'is'.

functions.note: Name the part you do not understand. 'I did not follow the second step' helps more than just 'I don't understand'.

functions.name: Asking for a favour

formal: I was wondering whether you could do me a favour.
Would you mind looking after my cat this weekend?
I hope you don't mind my asking, but could you lend me your notes?
neutral: Could you do me a favour?
Can you give me a lift to the airport?
Would you mind watering my plants?
informal: Can you do me a solid?
Any chance you could pick me up?
Could you cover for me for an hour?

responses: Sure, what do you need?
Of course, no problem.
I'd love to, but I'm busy that day.

example.en: Could you do me a favour?
Sure, what do you need?
Can you give me a lift to the airport on Friday?
Of course. What time is your flight?

avoid.wrong: Would you mind to help me?
avoid.right: Would you mind helping me?
avoid.why: After 'mind' we use the -ing form, not 'to' and the base verb.

functions.note: Say what you need and how long it takes. Make it easy to say no, and thank the person afterwards.

functions.name: Asking for someone's opinion

formal: May I ask what your view is on this?
What are your thoughts on the new schedule?
I would value your opinion on this matter.
neutral: What do you think about it?
How do you feel about the idea?
Do you think it's a good plan?
informal: So, what's your take?
Be honest, do you like it?
Thoughts?

responses: I think it's a good idea.
To be honest, I'm not sure.
I'd like some time to think about it.

example.en: We could move the meeting to Monday. What do you think about it?
I'm not sure. Monday is very busy for me.
How do you feel about Tuesday, then?
Tuesday is much better, thanks.

avoid.wrong: What do you think about of this idea?
avoid.right: What do you think about this idea?
avoid.why: After 'about' we do not add 'of'.

functions.note: 'What do you think?' asks for an opinion. 'What do you think of it?' asks if the person likes it. Both are common.

functions.name: Making a routine business phone call

formal: Good morning, this is Omar Hale from Brightway Logistics. I am calling about an order.
I am calling to confirm our meeting on Thursday.
Could you put me through to the accounts department, please?
neutral: Hello, I'm calling about the delivery date.
Could I speak to someone in sales, please?
I'm returning your call from this morning.
informal: Hi, it's Omar. Have you got a minute?
Just a quick call about tomorrow.
Hi, is now a good time?

responses: One moment, I'll put you through.
Yes, how can I help?
Can you hold, please?

example.en: Hello, I'm calling about the delivery date.
Of course. Could I have your order number?
Yes, it's 4471.
Thank you. It should arrive on Wednesday.

avoid.wrong: I call you for ask about the order.
avoid.right: I'm calling to ask about the order.
avoid.why: Use 'calling to' plus a base verb for purpose. 'For ask' is incorrect.

functions.note: State who you are and why you are calling in the first ten seconds. It saves time for both people.

functions.name: Changing an arrangement

formal: I am afraid I need to reschedule our meeting.
Would it be possible to move our appointment to next week?
Unfortunately, I will have to cancel. May I suggest a new date?
neutral: Can we change it to Thursday?
Something has come up, so I can't make it at four.
Could we put it back by an hour?
informal: Sorry, can we push it to Friday?
Something's come up. Rain check?
Can we do tomorrow instead?

responses: That's fine. What time suits you?
No worries, let's find another day.
Thanks for telling me early.

example.en: Something has come up, so I can't make it at four.
No worries. When would suit you?
Can we change it to Thursday?
Thursday is fine. Same time?

avoid.wrong: I cancel our meeting to Friday.
avoid.right: I'd like to move our meeting to Friday.
avoid.why: 'Cancel' means stop it completely. To change the day, use 'move' or 'change'.

functions.note: Tell people as early as possible and always offer a new time. This shows respect for their schedule.

functions.name: Changing the subject

formal: If I may, I should like to turn to another matter.
On a different note, have you seen the new report?
Before we finish, may I raise something else?
neutral: By the way, did you hear about the party?
Anyway, how is your new job?
Speaking of work, how is your project going?
informal: Oh, random, but did you see the match?
Anyway, enough about that!
Oh, that reminds me!

responses: No, tell me about it.
Sure, let's talk about that.
Oh yes, I wanted to ask you too.

example.en: And the traffic was terrible all week.
Anyway, how is your new job?
It's great, thanks. The team is friendly.
That's good to hear. Are you busy?

avoid.wrong: Now I talk about something else.
avoid.right: Anyway, let me ask you something else.
avoid.why: Use a signal word like 'anyway' or 'by the way', not a direct announcement.

functions.note: Use a small link phrase ('by the way', 'speaking of...') so the change does not feel sudden or rude.

functions.name: Checking that someone has understood

formal: Have I made myself clear?
Is everything clear so far, or shall I go over it again?
Would you like me to explain any part in more detail?
neutral: Does that make sense?
Do you follow me so far?
Is that clear?
informal: You with me?
Make sense?
Okay so far?

responses: Yes, that's clear, thank you.
Could you repeat the last step?
I think so. Can I check with an example?

example.en: So you open the form, then you sign at the bottom. Does that make sense?
Yes, but where do I find the form?
It's in the blue folder on my desk.
Okay, thank you.

avoid.right: Does that make sense?
avoid.why: 'Do you understand?' can sound like you doubt the person's ability. Check your own explanation instead.

functions.note: Ask about your explanation, not the listener. This keeps the other person comfortable about saying 'no'.

functions.name: Congratulating someone

formal: Please accept my warmest congratulations on your promotion.
I was delighted to hear of your success.
Many congratulations on this achievement.
neutral: Congratulations on the new job!
Well done on passing the exam!
I'm so happy for you.
informal: Nice one!
You did it! Brilliant!
Awesome news, so proud of you!

responses: Thank you so much!
Thanks, I couldn't have done it without help.
That's very kind of you.

example.en: I passed my driving test today!
Congratulations! I'm so happy for you.
Thanks. I was really nervous.
Well done. Let's celebrate this weekend.

avoid.right: Congratulations on your exam.
avoid.why: We use the plural 'congratulations' and the preposition 'on'.

functions.note: 'Congratulations' always ends in -s. Say it for success and good news, but not for birthdays: use 'Happy birthday'.

functions.name: Ending a conversation politely

formal: I am afraid I must leave now. It has been a pleasure talking to you.
Thank you for your time. I should let you get on.
It was a pleasure meeting you. I hope we speak again soon.
neutral: Well, I should get going. It was nice talking to you.
I'd better let you go.
Anyway, great to catch up!
informal: Right, I'd better dash.
Good to see you! Catch you later.
Okay, I'll let you get on. Bye for now!

responses: Nice talking to you too.
Take care, and see you soon.
Yes, let's keep in touch.

example.en: Well, I should get going. It was nice talking to you.
You too. Say hello to your family from me.
I will. Let's keep in touch.
Definitely. Take care!

avoid.right: I should get going. Bye.
avoid.why: 'Finish' sounds like ending a task. Use 'I should get going' or 'I have to go'.

functions.note: Give a short reason and say something warm at the end. Never just walk away in the middle of a sentence.

functions.name: Expressing preferences

formal: I would prefer to travel by train, if that is acceptable.
I would rather meet in the morning, if possible.
I find the second option more suitable.
neutral: I prefer tea to coffee.
I'd rather stay in tonight.
I like the red one better.
informal: I'm more of a cat person.
Give me the beach over the mountains any day.
I'd go for pasta, honestly.

responses: Okay, let's do that.
Me too. I like it better as well.
Really? I'd choose the other one.

example.en: Shall we go out or stay in tonight?
I'd rather stay in tonight. I'm tired.
Fine with me. I'll cook.
I'd go for pasta, honestly.

avoid.right: I prefer tea to coffee.
avoid.why: 'Prefer' goes with 'to', not 'than'. Use 'than' with 'rather' structures and comparatives.

functions.note: 'I prefer X to Y' compares two things. 'I'd rather' is followed by the base verb and has no 'to'.

functions.name: Expressing surprise and interest

formal: That is quite astonishing, I must say.
I had no idea. How interesting!
I must admit, that surprises me.
neutral: Really? I didn't know that.
Wow, that's amazing!
That's a surprise!
informal: No way!
Seriously? You're kidding!
Whoa, I never saw that coming.

responses: Yes, it's true!
I know, I couldn't believe it either.
I was surprised too.

example.en: I'm moving to Canada next month.
Really? I didn't know that!
I only decided last week.
Wow, that's amazing. Tell me everything.

avoid.right: I am surprised.
avoid.why: Use '-ed' for how you feel and '-ing' for what causes the feeling.

functions.note: Raise your voice at the end of 'Really?' to show real interest. A flat voice can sound like you do not believe the person.

functions.name: Giving advice

formal: If I were you, I would speak to your manager first.
I would strongly recommend taking some time off.
It might be wise to check the contract before signing.
neutral: You should see a doctor about that.
Why don't you try talking to her?
I think you'd better rest.
informal: Just go for it!
Honestly, I'd sleep on it.
You could always ask your mum.

responses: That's good advice, thanks.
I'll think about it.
I hadn't thought of that.

example.en: I have a headache every afternoon.
You should see a doctor about that.
Do you think it's serious?
Probably not, but it's better to check. Also, drink more water.

avoid.wrong: You should to see a doctor.
avoid.right: You should see a doctor.
avoid.why: After 'should' we use the base verb without 'to'.

functions.note: 'Should' and 'had better' are strong. Soft phrases like 'Why don't you' and 'If I were you' are kinder with friends.

functions.name: Giving and receiving compliments

formal: You gave a most impressive presentation.
I must say, your work is excellent.
That is a very elegant jacket.
neutral: I love your new haircut.
You did a great job on this.
That colour really suits you.
informal: Love your shoes!
You nailed it!
Wow, you look amazing.

responses: Thank you, that's kind of you.
Oh, thanks! I got it last week.
Thanks, you made my day.

example.en: I love your new haircut.
Oh, thanks! I got it last week.
That colour really suits you.
That's kind of you. Thank you.

avoid.right: Thank you, that's kind of you.
avoid.why: When someone compliments you, say thank you. Rejecting it can feel unfriendly.

functions.note: Compliment things people chose or worked on. Keep it about the thing, not about body or age.

functions.name: Giving your opinion

formal: In my view, the plan is a sound one.
As far as I am concerned, this is the best option.
I would say the proposal deserves serious consideration.
neutral: I think we should start early.
In my opinion, it's too expensive.
To me, the second one looks better.
informal: If you ask me, it's a waste of money.
Honestly, I'd go with the red one.
I reckon it'll be fine.

responses: That's a good point.
I see it a bit differently.
Why do you think so?

example.en: When should we begin the project?
I think we should start early.
Why? The deadline is two months away.
Because the first step usually takes longer than planned.

avoid.wrong: In my opinion, I think it is too expensive.
avoid.right: In my opinion, it is too expensive.
avoid.why: 'In my opinion' and 'I think' say the same thing, so use only one.

functions.note: Give a reason after your opinion with 'because'. It makes you sound thoughtful, not just negative or positive.

functions.name: Giving reasons and excuses

formal: I regret that I was unable to attend, owing to a family matter.
The delay was due to circumstances beyond my control.
I am afraid I could not finish it, as the system was down.
neutral: I'm late because the train was cancelled.
I couldn't come since I wasn't feeling well.
The reason is that I lost my keys.
informal: Sorry, got stuck in traffic.
My phone died, that's why I didn't reply.
I totally forgot, I was so busy.

responses: That's all right, thanks for letting me know.
Oh dear, are you okay now?
Next time, please call me.

example.en: Why weren't you at the meeting?
I couldn't come since I wasn't feeling well.
Oh dear, are you okay now?
Much better, thank you. Could you share the notes?

avoid.right: I'm late because the train was delayed.
avoid.why: 'Because' needs a main clause with it. 'Because' alone is not a full sentence.

functions.note: Give one short, true reason. Long explanations can sound like excuses, and sorry should come first.

functions.name: Handling a travel problem

formal: I would like to know what options are available, as my flight has been cancelled.
Could you tell me whether I am entitled to compensation?
I need to rebook, as I have missed my connection.
neutral: My train was cancelled. What should I do?
Can you put me on the next flight?
I've lost my luggage. Where do I report it?
informal: Ugh, we missed the bus. Now what?
Can you help? Our train's not showing up.
Any other way to get there?

responses: I'm sorry. I'll check what is available.
There's another train at six.
Please fill in this form, and we'll contact you.

example.en: My train was cancelled. What should I do?
I'm sorry. There's another one at six.
Is my ticket still valid for it?
Yes, just show it to the conductor.

avoid.right: I missed my flight.
avoid.why: You 'lose' things, such as luggage, but you 'miss' transport.

functions.note: Stay calm, explain the facts in one sentence, and ask a direct question. Staff can help faster this way.

functions.name: Interrupting politely

formal: Excuse me for interrupting, but may I add something?
If I may, I would like to say a word here.
Forgive me for cutting in, but there is a point I should raise.
neutral: Sorry to interrupt, but I have a question.
Can I just say something here?
Sorry, could I come in for a second?
informal: Hang on a sec!
Oh, can I jump in?
Wait, before you go on, can I say something?

responses: Of course, go ahead.
Sure, what is it?
Let me just finish this point, and then you can speak.

example.en: So the budget for next year will be about the same, and we will also...
Sorry to interrupt, but I have a question.
Of course, go ahead.
Does that budget include travel costs?

avoid.right: Sorry to interrupt, but I have a question.
avoid.why: Never order people to stop. Say sorry first, then state your reason.

functions.note: Wait for a short pause if you can. Raise a hand in a meeting, and always say what you want in few words.

functions.name: Leaving a phone message

formal: Could you please take a message for Mr Evans?
Would you ask her to call me back as soon as possible?
Please tell him that Ms Roy called about the invoice.
neutral: Can I leave a message, please?
Could you ask him to call me back?
Please tell her I called. My number is 555 0142.
informal: Can you tell Jo I rang?
Just ask her to text me back.
Tell him I'll try again later.

responses: Of course. Can I have your name and number?
I'll pass that on to her.
Shall I say what it is about?

example.en: Can I leave a message, please?
Of course. Can I have your name and number?
It's Lena Park, and my number is 555 0142.
Thanks. I'll pass that on to her.

avoid.right: Please tell him I called.
avoid.why: 'Tell' takes a person directly. We do not say 'say him'.

functions.note: Give your name, your number, and the reason in that order. Repeat the number slowly so it can be written down.

functions.name: Making a complaint

formal: I would like to make a complaint about the service I received.
I am afraid this is not what I ordered, and I would like it replaced.
I must say I am disappointed with the standard of the room.
neutral: Excuse me, there's a problem with my order.
I'd like to complain about the delay.
This isn't what I expected. Can you fix it?
informal: Hey, this isn't right.
Sorry, but I've been waiting ages.
Er, this is cold, actually.

responses: I'm very sorry. I'll sort it out right away.
Let me get the manager for you.
Would you like a refund or a replacement?

example.en: Excuse me, there's a problem with my order.
I'm sorry to hear that. What is the problem?
I asked for a vegetarian meal, but this has chicken in it.
I'm very sorry. I'll change it right away.

avoid.right: The service here is very slow.
avoid.why: Talk about the problem, not the person. 'Bad service' describes a thing, not a person.

functions.note: Stay calm, describe the problem, then say what you want. This works better than anger.

functions.name: Refusing a request politely

formal: I am afraid I will not be able to help on this occasion.
Thank you for asking, but I must decline.
I would love to, but I am unable to commit to that.
neutral: I'm sorry, but I can't do that.
I'd rather not, if that's okay.
Thanks for asking, but I'll have to say no.
informal: Sorry, no can do.
I'll pass this time.
Ah, not this time, sorry.

responses: No problem, I understand.
That's fine. Maybe next time.
Okay, I'll ask someone else.

example.en: Could you cover my shift on Saturday?
I'm sorry, but I can't do that. I have a family event.
No problem, I understand.
I could help on Sunday, if that's useful.

avoid.right: I'm sorry, but I'd rather not.
avoid.why: A bare 'no' with 'don't want' sounds blunt. Add 'sorry' and a softer verb form.

functions.note: Say sorry, give a short true reason, and offer another option if you can. This keeps the relationship good.

functions.name: Showing sympathy

formal: I am so sorry to hear about your loss.
Please accept my sympathy for what you are going through.
That must be a very difficult time for you.
neutral: I'm really sorry to hear that.
That sounds awful. How are you feeling?
Oh no, that must be hard.
informal: Oh, that's rough.
Ugh, I feel for you.
I'm here if you want to talk.

responses: Thank you, that means a lot.
It's been tough, but I'm coping.
I appreciate you asking.

example.en: I didn't get the job I wanted.
Oh no, I'm really sorry to hear that.
Thanks. I thought the interview went well.
That sounds hard. I'm here if you want to talk.

avoid.wrong: I am sorry for your news.
avoid.right: I am sorry to hear your news.
avoid.why: We say 'sorry to hear' for bad news. 'Sorry for' is used for something you did.

functions.note: Listen first and do not rush to give advice. A short, kind sentence works better than a long speech.

functions.name: Making special requests in a restaurant

formal: I wonder whether it would be possible to have the sauce on the side.
Would it be possible to seat us by the window?
I have a nut allergy. Could you check the ingredients for me?
neutral: Could I have the salad without onions?
Is it possible to swap the chips for rice?
Do you have a vegetarian option?
informal: Can I get that without cheese?
Any chance of a table outside?
Could we have extra bread?

responses: Of course, no problem.
I'll ask the kitchen.
I'm afraid we can't change that, but we can offer another dish.

example.en: Could I have the salad without onions?
Of course. Would you like anything else changed?
Is it possible to swap the chips for rice?
I'll ask the kitchen and let you know.

avoid.wrong: I want the soup but not with the carrots.
avoid.right: Could I have the soup without carrots?
avoid.why: Use 'without' for something you do not want, and 'Could I have' for a polite request.

functions.note: Mention allergies clearly and early. For taste preferences, ask 'Is it possible...?' so the staff can say yes or offer another option.

functions.name: Starting small talk with a stranger

formal: Excellent weather we are having, is it not?
Have you travelled far to attend this event?
May I ask how you know our host?
neutral: Lovely day, isn't it?
Have you been here before?
Is this your first time in the city?
informal: Crazy weather, huh?
So, what brings you here?
Hey, nice bag. Where's it from?

responses: Yes, it's beautiful. Are you from here?
No, it's my first visit. And you?
I'm here for work. How about you?

example.en: Lovely day, isn't it?
It really is. Are you from around here?
No, I'm just visiting. Have you been here before?
Many times. I can recommend a few places.

avoid.wrong: How old are you and how much do you earn?
avoid.right: What do you do for work?
avoid.why: Avoid personal questions about age or money with strangers. Choose safe topics: weather, travel, work.

functions.note: Start with something you both share, like the place or the weather. Ask open questions, then listen and respond.

functions.name: Warning someone

formal: Please be advised that the floor is wet.
I must warn you that the road ahead is closed.
I would urge you to keep your belongings with you.
neutral: Be careful, the step is loose.
Watch out for the traffic.
I wouldn't go that way. It's dangerous.
informal: Careful!
Heads up, the boss is coming.
Mind the gap!

responses: Thanks for the warning.
Oh, I didn't see that.
Thanks, I'll be careful.

example.en: Be careful, the step is loose.
Oh, thanks. I didn't see that.
Someone fell there yesterday.
I'll tell the manager about it.

avoid.right: Watch out!
avoid.why: 'Attention' alone sounds like a command. Use 'watch out' or 'be careful' with a reason.

functions.note: For real danger, shout the short form first (Watch out!) and explain after. The long forms are for notices and calm talk.

functions.name: Agreeing with reservations

formal: I broadly agree, although I have one or two concerns about the cost.
In principle I support the idea, provided that the risks are managed.
I am largely in favour, but I would want further assurances.
neutral: I agree up to a point, but it's quite expensive.
That sounds good, as long as we have enough time.
I'm mostly on board, though I'm not sure about the date.
informal: Yeah, I'm in, just not thrilled about the date.
Sure, but only if it doesn't run late.
I'm kind of up for it, with a few doubts.

responses: Fair enough. What worries you most?
Good point. We can adjust the date.
So you're happy if we limit the budget?

example.en: I suggest we hold the event outdoors.
I agree up to a point, but it's quite expensive.
We could ask a local company to sponsor it.
That sounds good, as long as we have enough time.

avoid.right: I agree up to a point, but I have one concern.
avoid.why: Name the part you agree with and the exact doubt. A plain 'yes, but no' confuses the listener.

functions.note: Say what you accept before naming the condition. 'As long as' and 'provided that' introduce the condition clearly.

functions.name: Answering job interview questions

formal: I have six years of experience in project management, during which I led teams of up to twelve.
One of my main strengths is the ability to remain calm under pressure.
In my previous role, I was responsible for reducing delivery times by twenty percent.
neutral: I'm good at solving problems, and I enjoy learning new things.
My biggest achievement was launching a new product on schedule.
I'd like to grow in this field and take on more responsibility.
informal: Basically, I like to get things done.
I'm a quick learner, to be honest.
The team I led was great, and we hit every target.

responses: Can you give an example?
What did you learn from that?
Why do you want to work here?

example.en: What is your biggest achievement so far?
My biggest achievement was launching a new product on schedule.
Can you give an example of a problem you solved?
Yes. A supplier failed, so I found another within two days.

avoid.wrong: I am a hard-working, and honest and kind.
avoid.right: I am hardworking, honest and kind.
avoid.why: A list uses commas between items and 'and' before the last, with no extra 'and' or comma.

functions.note: Use a short example for each claim: situation, action, result. Specific facts are more convincing than adjectives.

functions.name: Describing trends in data

formal: Sales rose steadily throughout the second half of the year.
There was a marked decline in revenue after March.
Output remained stable at approximately two hundred units.
neutral: Prices went up sharply last year.
The number of users fell slightly in June.
Profits stayed about the same.
informal: Sales shot up in the spring.
It's been slowly going downhill.
Numbers really took off in July.

responses: What caused the rise?
Is that rate expected to continue?
How does that compare with last year?

example.en: Prices went up sharply last year.
What caused the rise?
Mostly energy costs, and the number of users fell slightly in June.
Is that fall expected to continue?

avoid.right: Sales increased by 20 percent.
avoid.why: Use the active past simple, 'increased', for a change that already happened. The passive form is wrong here.

functions.note: Say the direction (rose), the speed (sharply or slowly) and the size (by ten percent). 'Rise' has no object; 'raise' does.

functions.name: Disagreeing politely

formal: I see your point, but I am inclined to take a different view.
With respect, I am not convinced that this is the best approach.
I understand where you are coming from; however, I would argue otherwise.
neutral: I see what you mean, but I think it's risky.
That's true, but have you thought about the cost?
I'm not sure I agree, to be honest.
informal: Yeah, but is that really fair?
Hmm, I'd say the opposite.
I get that, but I'm not buying it.

responses: That's a fair challenge.
Hmm, I hadn't looked at it that way.
Let's hear your reasons.

example.en: We should cut the training budget.
That's true, but have you thought about the cost of mistakes?
Hmm, I hadn't looked at it that way.
Perhaps we could reduce it by ten percent instead.

avoid.right: I see your point, but I'm not sure I agree.
avoid.why: Acknowledge the other view first, then add 'but'. This keeps the tone respectful.

functions.note: Agree with a small part, then disagree with the main point. Give your reason right after, so it does not sound personal.

functions.name: Making a request in a formal email

formal: I am writing to enquire whether it would be possible to extend the submission date.
I would be grateful if you could send me the revised contract by Friday.
Please could you confirm receipt of this email at your earliest convenience?
neutral: I'd like to ask if you could send me the schedule.
Could you let me know when the report will be ready?
I'm writing to check the status of my order.
informal: Quick question: can you send me the file?
Could you share the link when you get a chance?
Hi Sam, any news on the invoice?

responses: Thank you for your email. I will send it today.
I am afraid that will not be possible.
I will check and reply by Thursday.

example.en: I am writing to enquire whether it would be possible to extend the submission date.
Thank you for your email. How long would you need?
Another week would be ideal.
I will check and reply by Thursday.

avoid.wrong: I want you send me the contract.
avoid.right: I would be grateful if you could send me the contract.
avoid.why: 'I want' is too direct in a formal email, and 'want you send' is ungrammatical.

functions.note: Begin with the reason for writing, make one clear request and give a date. End with thanks, not an apology.

functions.name: Giving bad news

formal: I regret to inform you that your application has not been successful.
I am afraid I have some difficult news to share.
Unfortunately, we have had to postpone the launch.
neutral: I'm sorry to say that the project's been cancelled.
I'm afraid I have some bad news.
I'm sorry, but it didn't work out.
informal: So, I've got some not-so-great news.
Heads up, it's not good.
I hate to say it, but they said no.

responses: Oh no, what happened?
Thank you for telling me directly.
What will happen next?

example.en: I'm afraid I have some bad news.
Oh no, what happened?
The client has decided to cancel the contract.
That's disappointing. What will happen next?

avoid.right: I'm afraid I have some difficult news for you.
avoid.why: Prepare the listener first with a warning phrase before giving the news. Sudden facts feel cruel.

functions.note: Give a short warning, then the facts, then what happens next. Do not hide the news in long explanations.

functions.name: Giving constructive feedback

formal: I would like to commend your thorough analysis; one area to strengthen is the conclusion.
Overall, the report is well structured. I would suggest adding more evidence in section two.
May I offer some observations that might help the next draft?
neutral: You did well on the data. Next time, try to make the summary shorter.
I liked your opening. The middle part could be clearer.
One thing that worked well was your use of examples.
informal: Loved the slides! Maybe cut a few words?
Nice work. Just tighten up the ending.
Great start. Could you add a bit more detail on cost?

responses: Thank you, that's really useful.
Can you show me an example of what you mean?
I'll work on that.

example.en: One thing that worked well was your use of examples.
Thank you. Is there anything I should improve?
The middle part could be clearer. Try one idea per paragraph.
That's really useful. I'll work on that.

avoid.wrong: Your work is bad, change it all.
avoid.right: The middle part could be clearer.
avoid.why: Useful feedback is specific and describes the work, not the person.

functions.note: Start with something real that works, then name one change with a reason. Offer help to make it happen.

functions.name: Handling questions after a presentation

formal: Thank you for that question. I would be glad to elaborate.
That is a very good point. I will address it in a moment.
I am afraid I do not have that figure to hand, but I will follow up.
neutral: Good question. Let me think for a second.
Could you repeat the question, please?
I'm not sure, but I'll find out and get back to you.
informal: Ooh, good one.
Fair point, I hadn't thought of that.
No idea, honestly. I'll check.

responses: Thank you, that clears it up.
Could you give an example?
Can you send me the data later?

example.en: Does your method work with small samples?
Good question. Let me think for a second.
Of course, take your time.
I'm not sure, but I'll find out and get back to you.

avoid.right: Good question. Let me think for a second.
avoid.why: Thank the person and take a moment. Never judge a question aloud.

functions.note: Repeat or rephrase the question so everyone hears it. If you do not know, say so honestly and promise a follow-up.

functions.name: Inviting others to speak

formal: I would be interested to hear your views, Dr Walker.
Would anyone like to add anything at this stage?
May I invite those who have not yet spoken to share their thoughts?
neutral: What do the rest of you think?
Does anyone have anything to add?
I'd like to hear from Sam on this.
informal: Come on, you lot, what do you reckon?
Anyone want to chip in?
Don't be shy. What's your take?

responses: I'd like to add a point about cost.
I think we're missing one risk.
Just to build on that idea...

example.en: That's my summary. Does anyone have anything to add?
I'd like to add a point about cost.
Please go ahead. And what do the rest of you think?
We should hear from the sales team too.

avoid.right: I'd like to hear from Sam on this.
avoid.why: Use a name and an invitation. A command makes quiet people more nervous.

functions.note: Ask open questions and name quiet people kindly. Wait a few seconds in silence, as people often need time to think.

functions.name: Putting forward a proposal

formal: I would like to put forward a proposal for improving customer response times.
May I propose that we adopt a four-day trial period?
Let me outline a possible way forward.
neutral: I suggest we run a pilot first.
My proposal is to hire one more person.
What if we tried a different supplier?
informal: Here's an idea: let's try it for a month.
How about we split the work?
What if we just test it?

responses: That's an interesting idea. What would it cost?
I'd support that.
Could you put it in writing?

example.en: I suggest we run a pilot first.
That's an interesting idea. What would it cost?
Very little. We would only need two people for a month.
I'd support that. Could you put it in writing?

avoid.wrong: I propose you to change the supplier.
avoid.right: I propose that we change the supplier.
avoid.why: 'Propose' is followed by 'that' plus a clause, not by 'you to'.

functions.note: State the idea, the benefit and the cost briefly. Invite questions so the proposal feels shared.

functions.name: Moving between sections in a presentation

formal: That concludes the first part. Let us now turn to the financial results.
Having discussed the background, I would like to move on to our proposal.
This brings me to my next point.
neutral: Now let's look at the second part.
That's all for the overview. Next, the figures.
So, what does this mean for us?
informal: Okay, next up: the numbers.
Right, so that's the background. On to the fun bit.
Moving on, then.

responses: Could you go back to the last slide?
Is the next part longer?
That was clear. Please continue.

example.en: That's all for the overview. Next, the figures.
Before you do, could you go back to the last slide?
Of course. Is there something unclear?
Just the date on the chart. Thank you.

avoid.wrong: Now I speak about the second point.
avoid.right: Now let's look at the second point.
avoid.why: A clear signal like 'now let's look at' marks the new section better than a plain statement.

functions.note: Use short signpost phrases and pause briefly. Listeners can then follow the structure even if they were distracted.

functions.name: Negotiating a deadline

formal: Would it be possible to extend the deadline until the end of the month?
I would like to propose a revised timetable for delivery.
If we could have the data by Monday, we could meet the original date.
neutral: Is there any chance of a few more days?
I can finish by Friday if I get the files today.
Could we push the deadline back a week?
informal: Any wiggle room on the date?
Can I get till Monday?
If I get the files today, I'll be fine.

responses: I could give you until Wednesday.
The client needs it by Friday, I'm afraid.
What would you need to finish on time?

example.en: Is there any chance of a few more days?
The client needs it by Friday, I'm afraid.
I can finish by Friday if I get the files today.
Okay. I'll send them within the hour.

avoid.right: I cannot meet the deadline.
avoid.why: We 'meet' a deadline. 'Finish' is used for the work, not for the deadline.

functions.note: Offer a solution, such as what you need in return. Telling someone early is far better than missing a date.

functions.name: Negotiating a price

formal: Would you be willing to reduce the price if we order in bulk?
We would be prepared to proceed at a figure closer to two thousand.
Is there any flexibility on the quoted price?
neutral: Is that your best price?
Could you knock a bit off if I pay cash?
I can offer you eighty for it.
informal: Any chance of a discount?
Can you do it for fifty?
How about we meet in the middle?

responses: I could go down by ten percent.
I'm afraid that's the lowest I can go.
Let's meet in the middle, then.

example.en: Is that your best price?
It is, but I could go down by five percent.
If I pay cash, could you knock a bit off?
Okay, ten percent, and we have a deal.

avoid.wrong: Your price is too much, I give you half.
avoid.right: Is that your best price? I can offer you half.
avoid.why: A direct insult to the price starts a fight. Ask a question first, then make an offer.

functions.note: Never accept the first price. Offer something in return, like cash or a larger order, and be ready to walk away.

functions.name: Opening a meeting

formal: Good morning, everyone. Thank you all for coming; shall we begin?
I would like to welcome you and outline today's agenda.
As we are all here, let us make a start.
neutral: Okay, let's get started.
Thanks for coming. Today we need to cover three things.
Right, I think we can begin.
informal: Alright, everyone, shall we kick off?
Let's crack on, we've got a lot to cover.
So, quick one today. Let's go.

responses: Good, I've read the agenda.
Can we start with the budget?
Sorry I'm late. Where are we?

example.en: Thanks for coming. Today we need to cover three things.
Is the budget first on the agenda?
Yes, then the schedule, and finally next steps.
Good. I've read the notes.

avoid.right: Let's start the meeting now.
avoid.why: The object 'the meeting' follows the verb, and 'now' goes at the end.

functions.note: Welcome people, say the purpose, and give the time limit. This helps everyone focus from the start.

functions.name: Opening a presentation

formal: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for joining me today.
I would like to begin by outlining what I will cover in the next fifteen minutes.
It is a pleasure to be here to talk about our new approach.
neutral: Hello, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about our sales results.
My aim today is to show you three ways to save time.
Let me start with a quick question.
informal: Hi all, thanks for coming!
So, today it's all about how we can work smarter.
Right, let's dive in.

responses: That sounds useful.
Could you share the slides afterwards?
I'm looking forward to it.

example.en: Hello, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about our sales results.
Will you cover the regional figures as well?
Yes, in the second half, after the overview.
Good. I'm looking forward to it.

avoid.wrong: Today I will speak you about my topic.
avoid.right: Today I'm going to talk to you about my topic.
avoid.why: We 'talk to' people 'about' a subject. 'Speak you' is incorrect.

functions.note: Greet, say what you will cover and how long it takes. An opening question or story helps keep attention.

functions.name: Persuading someone

formal: I would encourage you to consider the long-term benefits of this approach.
May I draw your attention to what we stand to gain?
I am confident you will find this option worthwhile.
neutral: Just think how much time we would save.
I really think it's worth trying.
What have we got to lose?
informal: Come on, it'll be fun!
Trust me, you won't regret it.
Go on, give it a go.

responses: You've almost convinced me.
Okay, let's give it a try.
I'm still not sure, to be honest.

example.en: I really think it's worth trying a new supplier.
But the old one has never failed us.
Just think how much time we would save.
You've almost convinced me. Show me the numbers.

avoid.wrong: You must do this, I order you.
avoid.right: I really think it's worth trying.
avoid.why: Persuading means giving reasons and benefits, not giving orders.

functions.note: Point out benefits for the other person, not only for yourself. A question such as 'What have we got to lose?' invites them to agree.

functions.name: Resolving a misunderstanding

formal: I think there may have been a misunderstanding. Allow me to clarify what I meant.
I apologise if I was unclear. What I intended to say was that the deadline is flexible.
It seems we have been at cross purposes.
neutral: Sorry, I think we're talking about different things.
I didn't mean it that way.
Let me explain what I meant.
informal: Oh, I think we got our wires crossed.
Hang on, that's not what I meant.
Ah, so we were on different pages!

responses: Oh, I see now. Thanks for explaining.
That makes sense. Sorry about that.
So you meant next Friday?

example.en: Sorry, I think we're talking about different things.
Possibly. I thought you wanted the report today.
No, I meant by next Friday. Let me explain what I meant.
Oh, I see now. Thanks for explaining.

avoid.right: I don't think I explained it clearly.
avoid.why: Take responsibility for the unclear message, not only the listener's. It lowers tension.

functions.note: Do not decide who is at fault. Say what you meant, ask what they understood, then agree on the next step.

functions.name: Responding to a complaint

formal: Thank you for bringing this to our attention. I sincerely apologise for the inconvenience.
I understand your frustration, and I would like to resolve this immediately.
We take your concerns seriously and will investigate without delay.
neutral: I'm really sorry about that. Let me see what I can do.
I can see why you're upset.
Let me look into it for you.
informal: Oh no, my bad. Let me fix that.
Yeah, that's not on. I'll sort it.
Sorry about that, give me a minute.

responses: Thank you, I appreciate that.
How long will it take?
I'd like a refund, please.

example.en: My order arrived damaged, and nobody answered my emails.
I can see why you're upset. Let me look into it for you.
How long will it take?
I'll send a replacement today and call you tomorrow.

avoid.right: I'm sorry about that. Let me look into it.
avoid.why: Blaming the customer, even when true, makes the problem bigger. Show you care first.

functions.note: Apologise, show you understand, then act. Customers want a result more than an explanation.

functions.name: Softening an opinion with hedging

formal: It could be argued that the timeline is somewhat optimistic.
I tend to think that the data may not support that conclusion.
To some extent, I would say the approach is a little risky.
neutral: I'm not sure it's the best idea.
It seems to me that we need more time.
Perhaps we're being a bit hasty.
informal: Kind of feels rushed, if you ask me.
I dunno, it's a bit much.
Might be just me, but it seems off.

responses: That's a fair point.
I see what you mean. Why do you say that?
Could you give an example?

example.en: We'll launch in two weeks.
Perhaps we're being a bit hasty.
Really? The product is nearly ready.
It seems to me that we need more testing.

avoid.right: I'm not sure the plan is realistic.
avoid.why: Hedging with 'I'm not sure' or 'a bit' keeps the point but removes the insult.

functions.note: Hedges such as 'seems', 'tend to', 'a little' make an opinion sound open to discussion. Do not use too many in one sentence.

functions.name: Speculating about causes

formal: It is conceivable that the delay was caused by a technical fault.
One possible explanation is that demand fell unexpectedly.
It may well be that the figures were entered incorrectly.
neutral: It could be because of the weather.
Maybe they changed their plans.
I suppose the traffic might have held him up.
informal: Must've been the rain, I guess.
I'd say it's down to the new boss.
Probably just a glitch.

responses: That's possible. Let's check.
I doubt it. The weather was fine.
Could be. Did anyone ask them?

example.en: Why hasn't the delivery arrived?
It could be because of the weather.
I doubt it. It's sunny in the north.
Maybe they changed their plans. Let's call them.

avoid.right: It must have rained yesterday.
avoid.why: For a past guess, use 'must have' plus a past participle.

functions.note: 'Must' is a strong guess, 'may' and 'could' are weaker. For the past, use have + participle: might have missed it.

functions.name: Summarising decisions and next steps

formal: To summarise, we have agreed to postpone the launch until June.
Let me recap the action points before we close.
In conclusion, Anna will draft the report, and Luis will review it by Friday.
neutral: So, to sum up, we're going ahead with option B.
Let's go over what we decided.
The next steps are clear: Maya sends the draft, and we meet on Tuesday.
informal: Okay, so basically we're doing B.
Quick recap: Sam does the budget, I do the slides.
So that's sorted, right?

responses: That matches my notes.
I think we also agreed on the budget.
Who sends the minutes?

example.en: So, to sum up, we're going ahead with option B.
That matches my notes. Who sends the minutes?
I will, by tomorrow morning.
Great. And Maya sends the draft on Friday.

avoid.wrong: In resume, we will do it.
avoid.right: To sum up, we will do it.
avoid.why: 'Resume' is not used to conclude in English. Use 'to sum up' or 'to summarise'.

functions.note: Name each action, the person responsible and the date. A written follow-up after the meeting makes it stronger.

functions.name: Taking and holding the turn

formal: If I may, I would like to respond to that point.
May I come in here? I have a relevant example.
Could I just finish what I was saying before we move on?
neutral: Can I just add something here?
Let me finish my point, please.
I'd like to say something about that.
informal: Hold on, let me finish.
Can I just jump in?
One more thing before you move on.

responses: Sure, go ahead.
Sorry, please carry on.
Yes, you were saying?

example.en: So the price has to go down, and we should also change the colour...
Can I just add something here?
Sure, go ahead.
The price is already the lowest in the market.

avoid.right: Let me finish my point, please.
avoid.why: Claim your turn by saying what you want to do, not by criticising the speaker.

functions.note: Use a short signal like 'Can I just add...' to enter. To keep your turn, say 'Let me finish' and carry on at an even pace.

functions.name: Adjusting formality to the audience

formal: I would be most grateful if you could consider this at your convenience.
Might I suggest that we revisit this at the next meeting?
I am writing further to our earlier correspondence.
neutral: Could you take a look at this when you can?
Shall we come back to this next time?
Following up on my last email.
informal: Can you have a quick look when you get a sec?
Let's pick this up next time.
Just chasing up my last message.

responses: Sure, I'll look at it today.
Of course, no rush.
Thanks for the reminder.

example.en: Could you take a look at this when you can?
Sure, I'll look at it today.
Thanks. For the director, I'll rewrite it more formally.
Good idea. Shall we come back to the wording tomorrow?

avoid.wrong: Hey dude, please find attached my CV for consideration.
avoid.right: Dear Ms Reid, please find my CV attached.
avoid.why: Informal greetings and a formal request clash. Keep the whole message at one level, suited to the reader.

functions.note: Think about who reads it: their status, how well you know them, and the purpose. In doubt, be slightly more formal.

functions.name: Announcing a change to a team

formal: I wish to inform you that, with effect from March, the department will be restructured.
It is my responsibility to let you know of a significant change to our working arrangements.
Following careful consideration, the board has decided to relocate the office.
neutral: I wanted to tell you all about a change coming next month.
From next week, we'll be using a new system.
I know this is a surprise, so I'd like to explain the reasons.
informal: Right, so there's a bit of news.
Heads up, things are going to look different soon.
Quick update: we're switching tools.

responses: Why has this been decided?
How will it affect my team?
When will we get more details?

example.en: From next week, we'll be using a new system.
How will it affect my team?
Training starts Monday, and the old system will run in parallel for a month.
That helps. When will we get more details?

avoid.wrong: We decided and you must do it, no questions.
avoid.right: I know this is a surprise, so I'd like to explain the reasons.
avoid.why: Explain why and invite questions. A change announced without reasons creates fear and rumours.

functions.note: Give the news first, then the reason, the impact and the next steps. Allow time for questions and acknowledge concerns.

functions.name: Buying time to think

formal: That is an important question, and I would like a moment to consider it carefully.
May I come back to you on that once I have looked at the figures?
Allow me a moment to gather my thoughts.
neutral: Let me think about that for a second.
Give me a minute to work that out.
That's a tough one. Can I get back to you?
informal: Hmm, good question.
Hang on, let me get my head round that.
Ooh, let me think.

responses: Of course, take your time.
No rush at all.
Could you let me know by Friday?

example.en: Would you consider moving to our Berlin office?
That's a tough one. Can I get back to you?
Of course. Could you let me know by Friday?
Yes, I'll give you an answer then.

avoid.right: Let me think about that for a second.
avoid.why: Silence filled with 'uh' sounds nervous. A clear phrase shows you are thinking, not lost.

functions.note: A short phrase gives you time and shows respect for the question. Always give a clear time when you will answer.

functions.name: Challenging a claim

formal: What evidence do you have to support that claim?
I would question whether that conclusion follows from the data.
Surely that generalisation needs to be tested against the facts.
neutral: How do you know that's true?
Where does that figure come from?
Is that really the case?
informal: Says who?
Really? Where did you hear that?
Got any proof?

responses: That's from last year's national survey.
Fair question. I'll check the source.
Good point. It may be less certain than I said.

example.en: Everyone knows that shorter meetings are always more productive.
Where does that figure come from?
It's from a study I read last year.
Could you send me the link? I'd like to see the sample size.

avoid.right: How do you know that's true?
avoid.why: Question the evidence, not the speaker's honesty. Calling someone a liar ends the discussion.

functions.note: Ask for the source or the reasoning rather than saying 'wrong'. A calm question makes weak claims fall on their own.

functions.name: Conceding a point gracefully

formal: I must concede that you are right about the costs.
On reflection, that is a valid criticism, and I accept it.
I stand corrected; the data does point the other way.
neutral: Okay, you've got a point there.
Fair enough, I hadn't thought about that.
I'll give you that one.
informal: Alright, you got me.
Ha, fair cop.
Okay, okay, point taken.

responses: Thank you. That helps us move forward.
No harm done. It was an easy mistake.
Glad we agree on that.

example.en: Your forecast ignores the seasonal drop in spring.
Okay, you've got a point there.
So the real figure might be lower.
Fair enough, I hadn't thought about that. I'll rework the numbers.

avoid.wrong: Yes, I am wrong, I am very stupid.
avoid.right: Fair enough, you've got a point there.
avoid.why: Conceding is calm and short. Excessive self-criticism makes the conversation uncomfortable.

functions.note: Concede one point clearly and then return to your main argument if needed. It shows confidence, not weakness.

functions.name: Critiquing a study or proposal

formal: While the proposal is ambitious, its assumptions about uptake appear insufficiently justified.
The methodology is largely sound; however, the sample size limits how far the findings can be generalised.
One weakness is the absence of a clear plan for evaluating outcomes.
neutral: The idea is promising, but the evidence is thin.
I like the goal, though the budget seems unrealistic.
What's missing is a comparison with existing methods.
informal: Great concept, but the numbers don't add up.
It's a bit hand-wavy in the middle.
Cool idea, but who pays for it?

responses: That's a fair criticism. I'll revise it.
We did consider that, but the data was limited.
Could you suggest how to strengthen it?

example.en: The idea is promising, but the evidence is thin.
That's a fair criticism. We only had a small sample.
What's missing is a comparison with existing methods.
Good point. I'll add one in the next version.

avoid.wrong: This proposal is a joke and has nothing good.
avoid.right: The idea is promising, but the evidence is thin.
avoid.why: A useful critique names both a strength and a specific weakness. Mockery gives the author nothing to improve.

functions.note: Be specific: what is weak, why it matters, and how it could be improved. Balance your comments with real strengths.
