functions.name: Declining a request from a senior colleague

formal: I appreciate you thinking of me, but I do not have the capacity to take this on without affecting my current commitments.
I would be glad to help, though I would need to postpone another priority. Which would you prefer?
I am afraid I cannot commit to that deadline, but I could deliver a partial version by Friday.
neutral: I'd like to help, but my schedule is full this week.
I can do it if we move something else. What's most important?
Could I suggest someone better placed to do this?
informal: I'd love to, but I'm swamped right now.
Can it wait till Monday?
Honestly, I'm stretched. Could Alex take it?

responses: I see. Let's look at who has time.
That's fair. What can you manage?
Thank you for being honest.

example.en: Could you prepare the board report by Thursday?
I can do it if we move something else. What's most important?
The board report. Move the training plan.
Understood. I'll start this afternoon.

avoid.right: I can do it if we move something else.
avoid.why: With a senior colleague, show the limit and offer a solution instead of a flat refusal.

functions.note: Thank them, explain your workload in facts, and offer an alternative. Let the senior person decide what comes first.

functions.name: Defusing a conflict

formal: I appreciate that this is a sensitive matter. Perhaps we could take a step back and consider common ground.
I understand your frustration, and I would like us to resolve this constructively.
May I suggest we pause and approach this calmly?
neutral: Let's take a breath and start again.
I don't want us to fall out over this.
Can we agree on what we both want?
informal: Whoa, let's calm down a second.
Hey, we're on the same side here.
Look, I don't want to argue.

responses: You're right. I'm sorry I raised my voice.
Okay, let's talk it through.
I want to fix this too.

example.en: You never tell me anything until it's too late.
Let's take a breath and start again.
Fine. I just felt left out of the decision.
I understand. Can we agree on how to share updates from now on?

avoid.right: Let's take a breath and start again.
avoid.why: Telling an angry person to 'calm down' often makes them angrier. Use 'let's' to include yourself.

functions.note: Lower your voice, use 'we', and name the shared goal. Do not argue about who started it.

functions.name: Expressing degrees of certainty

formal: It is virtually certain that the figures will be revised downward.
There is a reasonable likelihood that the merger will go ahead, though nothing is guaranteed.
It seems highly improbable that the results were affected.
neutral: I'm fairly sure they'll agree.
It's quite likely to rain tomorrow.
I doubt that it will work.
informal: Bet you it'll sell out.
Pretty sure it's fine.
No chance they'll say yes.

responses: How certain are you?
What makes you so sure?
I'd be more cautious than that.

example.en: Will the client accept our offer?
I'm fairly sure they'll agree, but their finance director is cautious.
How certain are you about her?
Not very. I'd say it's about seventy percent likely.

avoid.wrong: It is sure that he will come.
avoid.right: He is sure to come.
avoid.why: 'It is sure that' is not a natural pattern. Use 'He is sure to' or 'It is certain that'.

functions.note: Match the strength of your words to the evidence: certain, likely, possible, doubtful. Overstating certainty can cost you trust later.

functions.name: Disagreeing diplomatically in a debate

formal: I take your point, yet I wonder whether the evidence quite supports such a firm conclusion.
With the greatest respect, I would suggest that the argument overlooks one important factor.
I am not entirely persuaded, if I may say so, that the policy will achieve its aim.
neutral: I see where you're coming from, but I'd look at it differently.
That's a fair argument, though it doesn't match what I've seen.
I'm not convinced that's the whole picture.
informal: Fair enough, but I think that's missing something.
Hmm, I'd push back on that a little.
Come on, is that really the case?

responses: That is a fair challenge. Let me reconsider.
Perhaps, but can you point to evidence?
I'd welcome another view on this.

example.en: Surely remote work always raises productivity.
That's a fair argument, though it doesn't match what I've seen.
Really? The surveys are quite clear.
I'm not convinced that's the whole picture. Junior staff often struggle.

avoid.wrong: I am totally against with your idea.
avoid.right: I'm not convinced by your idea.
avoid.why: 'Against' does not take 'with', and it sounds extreme in a debate. Use 'not convinced' for a softer, more precise statement.

functions.note: Challenge the argument, not the person. Acknowledge what is valid, then say what is missing, and back it with a concrete reason.

functions.name: Using light teasing and humour

formal: I hesitate to mention it, but I believe someone has been rather generous with the coffee budget.
Perhaps we might forgive the delay, given that it was, after all, the first in a decade.
If I may say so, your punctuality has been remarkable. Regrettably, it was last Tuesday.
neutral: Nice of you to join us. We've only been here an hour.
You and your famous sense of direction again.
Careful, he'll talk about football all night.
informal: Wow, you're actually on time. Who are you?
Oh, here comes the expert!
Mate, you've got to be joking.

responses: Ha, very funny.
Okay, I deserved that.
You're one to talk!

example.en: Nice of you to join us. We've only been here an hour.
Ha, very funny. The train was late.
Of course it was. It always is when you travel.
You're one to talk. You were late on Monday.

avoid.wrong: You are so fat, ha ha.
avoid.right: You and your famous sense of direction again.
avoid.why: Tease only about harmless habits, never about appearance, family or things the person cannot change.

functions.note: Tease only people who know you well and keep your tone warm, smiling and light. If they look uncomfortable, stop at once.

functions.name: Pitching an idea

formal: I would like to present an opportunity that could reduce our costs by a fifth within a year.
Allow me to outline a proposal which addresses a gap we have all noticed.
What I am proposing is a modest pilot with measurable results in ninety days.
neutral: Imagine cutting delivery time in half. That's what this does.
The problem is clear, and I think we have a simple solution.
Here's what we need: a small team and three months.
informal: Okay, picture this: no more manual reports.
So here's the thing: it saves us hours every week.
Give me two minutes and I'll show you why it's worth it.

responses: What would it cost to start?
Who else has tried this?
Send me a one-page summary.

example.en: Imagine cutting delivery time in half. That's what this does.
Interesting. What would it cost to start?
A small team and three months, with a pilot in one region.
Send me a one-page summary and I'll bring it to the board.

avoid.wrong: My idea is the best, you must believe me.
avoid.right: Here's what we need: a small team and three months.
avoid.why: A pitch is about the listener's gain and the next step, not just your confidence.

functions.note: Open with the problem, give the solution in one sentence, then state the benefit and what you need. Keep it brief and specific.

functions.name: Raising a performance issue

formal: I would like to discuss a concern about the recent quality of the reports.
I have noticed that several deadlines have been missed recently, and I would like to understand why.
Could we talk about how your workload is going and what support you may need?
neutral: I wanted to talk about the last three reports.
I've noticed a pattern with the deadlines. Can we talk it over?
I'd like to understand what's getting in the way.
informal: Got a minute? I want to check in about the project.
Can we chat about how things are going?
I've spotted a few issues. Let's go through them.

responses: I didn't realise it was a problem. Can you give examples?
I've been struggling with the workload.
What support would help?

example.en: I've noticed a pattern with the deadlines. Can we talk it over?
Of course. I've been struggling with the workload.
Thanks for being open. What support would help?
A clearer priority list, and perhaps fewer meetings.

avoid.wrong: You are lazy and your work is terrible.
avoid.right: I've noticed a pattern with the deadlines.
avoid.why: Describe what you saw, using facts. Labels such as 'lazy' start a defence, not a solution.

functions.note: Give one or two specific examples, ask for their view, and agree on a plan with a date. Do it in private.

functions.name: Answering a hostile question

formal: I understand why that concern is raised, and I would like to answer it directly.
The premise of that question is not one I would accept, but let me address the substance.
I think it is fair to say that the facts tell a rather different story.
neutral: I can see why you'd ask that, but I don't think it's accurate.
Let me be clear about what happened.
That's not how I'd describe it, and here's why.
informal: Well, that's one way of putting it.
I'd push back on that, if I may.
Hang on, that's not what I said.

responses: Then how do you explain the figures?
So you deny it completely?
Thank you, that's a clearer answer.

example.en: Isn't it true that you ignored every warning?
That's not how I'd describe it, and here's why.
Then how do you explain the figures?
Let me be clear about what happened. The warnings were reviewed within a week.

avoid.wrong: That is a stupid question and I won't answer.
avoid.right: That's not how I'd describe it, and here's why.
avoid.why: Attacking the questioner makes you look defensive. Correct the claim calmly and then give the facts.

functions.note: Stay calm, repeat nothing negative, and correct the premise before answering. Speak slowly. The audience judges your composure more than the question.

functions.name: Closing a high-level negotiation

formal: I believe we have reached terms that are acceptable to both parties, subject to the final contract.
Should your board approve these provisions, I am confident we can proceed to signature.
I would like to confirm our understanding before we formalise the agreement.
neutral: I think we have a deal, if we can agree on the last clause.
Let's confirm what we've agreed and get it in writing.
We're happy with these terms. Shall we shake on it?
informal: Okay, I think we're there.
Right, let's seal it.
Good, so we're good to go.

responses: Agreed. I'll ask our lawyers to draft it.
We still need to settle the last point.
Excellent. A pleasure doing business with you.

example.en: I think we have a deal, if we can agree on the last clause.
We can accept a thirty-day review period. Anything else?
No, that settles it. Let's confirm what we've agreed and get it in writing.
Agreed. I'll ask our lawyers to draft it.

avoid.wrong: We sign now, no more talk.
avoid.right: Let's confirm what we've agreed and get it in writing.
avoid.why: Closing is about checking that both sides understand the terms, not forcing a signature.

functions.note: Summarise the agreed points aloud before you close. Everything must be written down afterwards, as oral agreements can be misremembered.

functions.name: Conveying warmth or distance through word choice

formal: I should be most happy to assist, should you wish it.
It would be a great pleasure to welcome you to our next event.
I am afraid that falls outside what we are able to offer at present.
neutral: I'd be glad to help, just let me know.
It would be lovely to see you there.
Sadly, that's not something we can do right now.
informal: Of course, anything you need, just shout!
Honestly, it'd make my day if you came.
Yeah, no, that's not going to happen.

responses: That is very generous of you.
Thank you. I do appreciate the warmth.
I see. Perhaps another time.

example.en: I'd be glad to help, just let me know.
That's very generous of you. Could you review my draft?
Of course. Send it over, and I'll read it tonight.
Thank you. I do appreciate the warmth.

avoid.right: Sadly, that's not something we can do right now.
avoid.why: Plain, cold wording creates distance. Soft adverbs like 'sadly' and 'I'm afraid' keep the same message but a kinder tone.

functions.note: Warmth comes from words such as 'glad', 'lovely' and 'just let me know'. Distance comes from passive, impersonal forms like 'it is not possible'.

functions.name: Changing the topic gracefully

formal: Perhaps we might leave that matter there for now, and turn to something rather happier.
If you will excuse me for changing the subject, I was hoping to hear about your recent travels.
That reminds me of a question I have been meaning to put to you.
neutral: Shall we leave that for now? I'd love to hear about your trip.
Speaking of which, how is your sister getting on?
That's a bit of a heavy topic. What have you been reading lately?
informal: Anyway, enough doom and gloom. What's new with you?
Oh, before I forget, how was the wedding?
Right, change of subject: did you see the game?

responses: Of course. It was wonderful, actually.
Yes, let's do that.
Oh, that's a nice thing to ask about.

example.en: And the whole sale fell through, which has been exhausting.
Shall we leave that for now? I'd love to hear about your trip.
Of course. It was wonderful, actually.
Tell me about the first week.

avoid.wrong: I don't want to talk about this. New topic.
avoid.right: Shall we leave that for now? I'd love to hear about your trip.
avoid.why: A blunt order to change the topic sounds cold. Offer a new topic that the other person will enjoy.

functions.note: Acknowledge what was said, then offer a lighter topic as an invitation. Use it to protect people from awkward or painful subjects.

functions.name: Mediating tension in a group

formal: It seems to me that both of you are, in fact, concerned about the same outcome.
May I suggest that each of you set out the main points without interruption, and then we compare them?
I would like to propose that we consider what a fair solution would look like for everyone.
neutral: Let's hear both sides before we decide anything.
I think you each have a point.
What would a good result look like for you both?
informal: Okay, you two, let's slow down a bit.
Honestly, you're closer than you think.
Can we all just take a step back?

responses: I suppose we do want the same thing.
Fine, I'll listen first.
That sounds reasonable.

example.en: He never consults me before he changes the plan.
Let's hear both sides before we decide anything.
Fine, I'll listen first.
Thank you. Honestly, you're closer than you think.

avoid.wrong: You are both wrong, listen to me.
avoid.right: I think you each have a point.
avoid.why: A mediator stays neutral. Blaming both sides makes you a third opponent.

functions.note: Stay neutral, name what both sides share, and propose a process, such as taking turns. Do not decide who is right too early.

functions.name: Making a sensitive public statement

formal: We deeply regret the distress this incident has caused, and we are committed to a full and transparent review.
Our thoughts are with those affected, and we will share further information as soon as it is confirmed.
We take full responsibility for what has happened, and we are determined to put it right.
neutral: We're very sorry for what has happened and are looking into it.
Right now, our priority is supporting the people affected.
We'll update you when we know more.
informal: We know this isn't good enough, and we're sorry.
We messed up, and we're going to fix it.
Thanks for your patience while we sort this out.

responses: When will the results be published?
Will anyone be held accountable?
Thank you for being open about this.

example.en: Why did it take so long to inform customers?
We know this isn't good enough, and we're sorry.
Will anyone be held accountable?
Our priority is supporting those affected, and a full review will be published in March.

avoid.right: We take full responsibility for what has happened.
avoid.why: The passive without an agent sounds like avoiding blame. Public trust depends on taking responsibility.

functions.note: Lead with care for those affected, state the facts you are sure of, and avoid guessing. Promise only what you can do.

functions.name: Speaking on a special occasion

formal: It is both an honour and a privilege to stand before you on this remarkable occasion.
I should like to raise a glass to those whose generosity made tonight possible.
Please join me in a toast to the happy couple, wishing them many years of joy.
neutral: I'm so glad we could all be here tonight.
I'd like to say a few words about someone very special.
Let's raise a glass to a wonderful friend.
informal: Right, I promise to keep this short.
Okay, now it's time for the embarrassing stories.
Cheers, everyone! Here's to the best team.

responses: Hear, hear!
Cheers!
That was beautifully said.

example.en: I'd like to say a few words about someone very special.
Go on, we're all listening.
Let's raise a glass to a wonderful friend, who made us all better.
Hear, hear! Cheers!

avoid.wrong: Today we celebrate because the party is.
avoid.right: I'd like to say a few words about someone very special.
avoid.why: A speech needs a clear opening and a person or reason for the celebration. Do not begin with an empty explanation.

functions.note: Thank the host, tell one short personal story and end with a toast. Keep it under three minutes and speak slowly.

functions.name: Using understatement and irony

formal: The results were not entirely what we had hoped for, one might say.
It is hardly the most efficient arrangement we could have devised.
One could be forgiven for thinking the schedule was a little optimistic.
neutral: Well, that went well.
It's not exactly my favourite way to spend a Monday.
That's one way to do it.
informal: Oh, brilliant, just what I needed.
Not our finest hour, was it?
Well, that could've gone better.

responses: You could say that again.
Ha, a slight understatement.
Yes, it was rather grim, wasn't it?

example.en: The presentation crashed, the projector failed, and the client left early.
Not our finest hour, was it?
A slight understatement, I'd say.
Ha, you could say that again. Shall we regroup tomorrow?

avoid.wrong: This is the worst day, I am so very sad.
avoid.right: Well, that could've gone better.
avoid.why: English humour often says less than is meant. Direct strong emotion sounds dramatic, not witty.

functions.note: Irony says the opposite of what is meant, and understatement says less. Both depend on tone of voice. In writing, be careful, as it can be misread.
